the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as ​**Δῆλος**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"Clear, visible ‌(from ​δῆλος)"[^1].

The ​ASCII ‌form *delos* ​survives ‌only because ​the ‌early ​domain-name system ​could ​not carry ​diacritics; ​it is ‌a ​technological compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Dēlos** ‌recovers the ​vowel ​length of ‌the ‌original directly ‌in ​the address ​bar. ‌The ​original carries ​both ‌stress and ​vowel ​length, and ‌exactly ​one historically ‌valid ​Unicode restoration ​exists, ​which ​places the ‌name ‌in Tier ​1.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**d** ‌→ **D** ‌— ‌Delta
​- **e** ‌→ ​**ē** — ​Eta: ​long epsilon
‌- ​**l** → ​**l** ​— Lambda
‌- ​**o** ​→ **o** ​— ‌Short omicron
​- ‌**s** → ​**s** ‌— Sigma

​The ‌project holds ‌the ​domain ​**dêlos.com** (xn--dlos-gpa.com) ​as ​the canonical ‌home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sources.citation: Homeric Hymn to Apollo.
Thucydides.

overview.body:
**Dēlos** ​(*delos*) — ‌Where Apollo ‌Was ​Born — ​belongs ​to the ​Greek tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Birthplace ​of ‌Apollo". The ​name ‌means "Clear, ​visible (from ​δῆλος)"[^1].

​Dêlos is ​the ​smallest great ‌place in ​Greek ‌religion: a ​bare ‌rock of ​three square ‌miles ​that became ‌the ​holiest island ​in the ‌Aegean ‌— the ‌birthplace ​of Apóllōn ​and Ártemis ‌— ​and then, ​by ‌a turn ​of history, ​the ‌busiest free ​port ‌of the ​Hellenistic world.[^2]

​PuniCodex ​restores the ​name ‌as **Dēlos** ‌and serves ​its ‌temple at ​[dêlos.com](https://xn--dlos-gpa.com). ​The original ‌carries both ‌stress ‌and vowel ‌length, ​and exactly ‌one historically ​valid ​Unicode restoration ​exists, ‌which places ​the name ​in ​Tier 1. ‌The ​plain ASCII ​form *delos* ​survives ‌as a ​modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the ‌restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

domains.body:
Dêlos ​is the ‌smallest ‌great place ​in ​Greek religion: ​a ​bare rock ​of ‌three square ​miles ​that became ‌the ​holiest island ‌in ​the Aegean ‌— ​the birthplace ​of ​Apóllōn and ​Ártemis ​— and ‌then, ​by a ‌turn ​of history, ‌the ​busiest free ‌port ​of the ‌Hellenistic ​world.[^1]

### ​Birth ‌of the ‌Twins

‌Lētō, refused ​by ​every land ‌fearing ​Hēra, found ​refuge ‌on the ​floating ​isle — ‌and ​light was ‌born ​there twice.

​### ​Mount Kynthos

​The ‌island's single ‌hill, ​giving Apóllōn ‌his ​epithet Kynthios ​and ‌climbers the ‌Aegean's ‌best panorama.

‌### ​Terrace of ‌the ​Lions

The ​Naxian ​lions of ‌ca. ​600 BCE, ​still ​facing the ‌Sacred ​Lake they ​were ​carved to ‌guard.

​### The ‌Free ​Port

Rome's ‌gift ​of 166 ‌BCE: ‌a duty-free ​harbour ​that made ​Dêlos ​the entrepôt ‌of ‌the eastern ​Mediterranean.

mythology.body:
The Homeric ​Hymn to Apóllōn ‌gives the island ‌a voice: Dêlos speaks, ​fears the god's ​power, and is ​promised eternal fame ​if she receives ​his birth — the ‌founding charter of ​Aegean sanctity.[^1]

### ​The Island that ‌Said Yes (The ​Refuge)

Hounded by Hēra's ‌jealousy, the pregnant ​Lētō was refused ‌by every island ​and mainland city ​until barren, drifting Dêlos ​accepted her — ​asking only that ​Apóllōn build his ‌great temple there. ​Lētō swore by the ‌Styx, clasped a ​palm tree, and ‌after nine days ​of labour bore ‌Apóllōn and Ártemis between ​the mountain and ‌the lake.[^2]

### ​The Floating Isle ​Made Fast (The ‌Anchoring)

Pindar and ‌Callimachus preserve the tradition ‌that Dêlos once ​floated freely over ​the sea, visible ‌in no fixed ​place, until the twins' ​birth pinned her ‌down — Zeús ​fastened her with ​adamant chains to ‌the sea floor. Her ​other ancient name, ‌Astería ("the starry"), ​recalls the wandering ​light that became ​a fixed point.

### ​No Birth, No ‌Death (The Purifications)

‌To keep the ​god's birthplace pure, ‌Athens purified Dêlos twice: ​Peisístratos removed the ​graves visible from ‌the temple, and ‌in 426/5 BCE ‌the Athenians cleared ‌the whole island of ​burials and forbade ‌anyone to be ​born or to ​die there — ​the sick and pregnant ‌ferried to Rheneia. ​A law of ​hospitality: the island ​belonged to the ‌god alone.

### The ​Delian League (The ​Treasury)

After the ​Persian Wars, the ‌Greek alliance against ​Persia kept its common ‌treasury in Apóllōn's ​sanctuary on Dêlos ‌— the neutral ​sacred bank of ‌the Aegean. In 454 ‌BCE Athens moved ​the funds to ​the Parthenon, converting ​an alliance into ​an empire; the island's ‌political star faded ‌even as its ​sanctity endured.

topography.body: Dêlos ​is ‌a ‌granite ​rib of ​3.4 ​km² ​in ​the ‌centre ​of ​the ‌Cyclades: ​a harbour ‌bay ​on ‌the ​west, ​the ​Sacred ​Lake ​(drained ‌since 1925) ​and ‌the ​sanctuary ‌quarter ​on ‌the ​north, ‌the ​theatre district ​on ‌the ‌south, ‌and ​**Mount ​Kynthos** ‌(113 ​m) ​rising behind ‌— ​the ​island's ‌single ​height, ‌crowned ​by ​the sanctuary ​of ​Zeús ‌and ‌Athēnā ​Kynthioi. ‌Its ​neighbor ​**Rheneia**, ‌a walk ‌of ‌oars ‌away, ​served ‌as ​the ​necropolis-island ​after ‌the purifications. ​Barren ​of ​water ‌and ​soil, ​the ​island's ‌holiness ​was always ‌an ​act ‌of ​choice ‌rather ‌than ​of ​nature ​— exactly ​as ‌the ‌Hymn ​says.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/dɛ̂ː.los/** ​— ​Attic ​Greek.[^1]

‌For the ​modern ​speaker, ‌the closest ​approximation ‌is: ​DAY-los, ‌with the ​circumflexed ​long ​e of ​Δῆλος.

​Kindred ‌and ​historical forms ‌of ​the ‌name:

- ​**Greek** ‌— ​Δῆλος
‌- **Latin** ​— ​Delos
‌- **Owned ‌form** ‌— ​Dêlos

​Greek Δῆλος ‌scans ​with ​a long ‌eta ​— ​Dêlos ‌with the ​circumflex ‌marks ​the ​stressed long ​vowel ​of ‌the nominative ‌exactly ​as ‌ancient ​grammarians wrote ​it. ‌The ‌macron-only form ‌Dēlos ‌is ​the ‌standard academic ​fallback ​(LSJ ​convention); both ‌are ​defensible, ​and ​the circumflex ‌form ​is ​the owned ​primary. ‌Modern ​Greek ‌says Dhilos ​with ‌a ​fricative; the ‌ancient ‌quantity, ​not ​the modern ​sound, ​is ‌what the ‌restoration ​records.

sources.citation: Homeric Hymns, Oxford Classical Texts (Allen); Loeb, 550 BCE.

meditation.body:
Dêlos teaches ​that insignificance can ‌be chosen. A rock ‌with no water, ​no soil, and ​no harbour worth ​the name became the ​centre of a ​world because it ‌alone said yes ​— and then became ​rich because everyone ‌remembered that it ​had. Sanctuary and ‌market, poverty and ​splendour: the island holds ‌both without apology.

​The purifications are ​the island's strangest ​monument: a place so ​holy that birth ​and death were ‌exported to the ​neighboring rock, as if ‌the whole human ​cycle were too ‌profane for three ​square miles. Every protected ‌place since — ​every reserve, sanctuary, ‌and clean room ​— is Dêlos' logic: ​holiness as exclusion, ‌maintained by ferries. ‌And yet the ‌same island ran ​the ancient world's busiest ​slave market beside ‌the god's lake. ​Dêlos holds the ​contradiction without apology: the ‌purest sanctuary and ​the purest market ​were one town, ‌and the lions faced ​the lake through ‌all of it.

​That is why ​the ruin moves visitors ​as no bigger ​site can: the ‌wind, the lizards ‌on the fallen drums, ​the cisterns under ‌the mosaics — ​a whole civilization ​left on a ‌barren rock because one ‌god was born ‌there and everyone ‌agreed to remember. ​The unmoved island finally ‌stopped the ships, ​and kept the ​story.

Go there ​in the shoulder season, ‌when the boat ​from Mykonos is ​half empty: the ​lizards own the marble, ‌the wind owns ​the theatre, and ​the lions face ​the empty lake as ‌they have for ​twenty-six centuries — ‌the smallest great ​place in Greece, ‌keeping its appointment with ​the light.

Apollo's ‌island asks one ‌thing of every ​visitor: to remember that ​sanctity, like the ​god's birth, is ​chosen — and ‌then kept, at whatever ‌cost, by whoever ​said yes.[^1]
